name: Wakeout
summary: Wakeout turns movement into a single running number, Wake Out Watts, earned through short exercise breaks and measured against a daily goal that the user can set by difficulty. The goal on the account observed was already met on the first screen after subscribing, credited from Apple Health history the user had not generated inside the app, before any goal had been shown to them. A separate setting, described in the app as Active Pass, makes selected external apps pause until the user completes a movement break, but sits in settings rather than being introduced during onboarding. There is no free tier: the paywall cannot be dismissed, and every feature described here is available after the user subscribes.

writeup.observed: Wakeout turns movement into a single running number, Wake Out Watts, and asks the user to grow it toward a daily target rather than toward any one finish line. Completing a wakeout, a movement break built from 4 exercises of 15 seconds each, granted 50 watts in a pop up naming the move just finished, and the running total moved from 613 to 663 out of a 700 target in the same moment. That target comes from a difficulty setting rather than being fixed: easy, the default, sets an active goal of 500 watts with a stretch goal of 200 watts above it, and a cap of 150 watts an hour, described in the app's own copy as encouraging movement across the day rather than one intense session. The other 4 levels move the same two numbers together, from 400 and 100 on very easy up to 1100 and 400 on very hard. The total keeps a longer record too: a stats section shows total watts earned, watts earned in the current week, and the most watts reached in a single day, and an activity log breaks the day down hour by hour into the activities that produced the watts.
writeup.presented: The running total sits at the top of the home screen as a number out of the day's target, above a bar that fills toward it. A check mark partway along the bar marks the active goal, and the bar continues filling past that point toward the stretch target. The same number reappears in the pop up after every completed move, in a calendar on the progress screen, and in the watts stats and activity log sections.
writeup.noting: Wake Out Watts never convert into anything spendable. They only ever move toward the day's threshold, and the hourly cap works on the same principle: it slows how fast the total can climb rather than blocking any single action, which keeps the pressure on spreading movement through the day instead of finishing it in one sitting. Five difficulty levels turn the same design into five different daily targets rather than five different mechanics, so a user can change how hard the goal is to reach without changing what reaching it means.
findings: A completed move adds a fixed 50 watts to the running total, shown in the same pop up that names the move.
Five difficulty levels each pair an active goal with a separate stretch goal above it, from 400 and 100 watts on very easy to 1100 and 400 on very hard.
The easy default caps earning at 150 watts an hour, limiting how much of the day's target one burst of activity can fill.
The running total is also kept as a longer record, with a weekly figure and a single day high shown in a dedicated stats section.

writeup.observed: Wakeout recognizes the moment a user's watts cross a defined daily threshold, separately from the number simply rising. On the first screen after subscribing, a pop up read "daily goal achieved," with a notification stating "613 watts, like discovering a new planet, you've conquered your active goal." The same crossing is marked on the home screen as a check mark partway along the watts bar. A second, higher threshold sits above the first: onboarding showed a bar at 540 out of 700 with "160 watts to make it a super active day," and the progress screen keeps separate counters for active days, super active days, and sedentary days, alongside the longest streak reached at each level. Reaching that second threshold was not shown in the session, and the counters read zero super active days throughout.
writeup.presented: Crossing the first threshold produces a full screen pop up shown immediately, before the user had otherwise opened the app that day. Beyond that single moment, the state is kept quietly: the check mark on the home screen bar, a calendar on the progress screen recording which days were active, and the day-state counters described above.
writeup.noting: Two different thresholds sit on the same watts total, and only one of them is explained anywhere the session reached. Reaching the ordinary goal is celebrated immediately with a name for what happened, while super active status is only visible as a counter and a line of onboarding copy, with no equivalent celebration shown. That gap leaves a second goal standing behind the first, visible but undefined, once the user has already met the one that was explained.
findings: Crossing the daily goal produces a full screen pop up naming the achievement, distinct from the bar simply filling further.
A second, higher threshold, called a super active day, is tracked in the same counters but was not explained anywhere in the session.
The progress screen keeps separate day-state counts for sedentary, active, and super active days, plus the longest streak reached at each level.
The threshold crossed in the session was already met on the first screen after subscribing, from movement recorded before that point.

writeup.observed: Wakeout counts a streak of days on which the user reached the daily watts goal, sitting beside the goal total rather than tracking its own separate action. After the goal was reached, the app recorded a one day streak, shown on the home screen next to the watts total, and a section on the progress screen headed "activity goal streak, reach your goal, increase your streak" kept the same count alongside a calendar and a longest streak record. That day was credited from movement recorded across the day, including a gym session, rather than from an action taken inside the app itself. Settings also carries a control described as "take a day off," which turns off notifications for a chosen number of days under copy reading "don't break your streak."
writeup.presented: The streak count sits at the top of the home screen beside the watts total, and reappears inside the activity goal streak section on the progress screen and as a longest streak figure in the watts stats. The day off control sits in settings, framed around protecting the streak rather than around notifications alone.
writeup.noting: The qualifying event for the streak is reaching the day's watts goal, the same event the app already celebrates on its own, so the streak adds a second, cumulative layer on top of a threshold that is already being tracked rather than introducing a separate action to perform. Framing the day off control around not breaking the streak, rather than only around muting notifications, keeps the streak named as the thing being protected even where the underlying continuity rule is not shown.
findings: A day counts toward the streak by reaching the watts goal for that day, the same event that triggers the goal achieved pop up.
The streak observed was credited from movement recorded during the day, including a gym session, not from completing a wakeout inside the app.
A longest streak figure is kept separately in the watts stats, alongside the running day count shown on the home screen.
The day off control in settings is framed around not breaking the streak rather than only around pausing notifications.
